'''Eluvathingal Devassy Jemmis''' (born 31 October 1951) is a professor of theoretical chemistry at the [[Indian Institute of Science]], Bangalore, India. He was the founding director of [[Indian Institute of Science Education and Research]], Thiruvananthapuram [[Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Thiruvananthapuram|(IISER-TVM)]]. His primary area of research is [[Quantum chemistry|applied theoretical chemistry]] with emphasis on structure, bonding and reactivity, across the periodic table of the elements. Apart from many of his contributions to applied theoretical chemistry,<ref name=jemmis-research-expedition>{{cite journal|title=Research expedition of Prof. Eluvathingal D. Jemmis|author1=Prasad V. Bharatam|author-link=Prasad V. Bharatam|author2=Gernot Frenking |author3=G. Narahari Sastry |journal=Theor Chem Acc|year=2012|volume=131|issue=3 |pages=1–2|doi=10.1007/s00214-012-1164-4|doi-access=free}}</ref> an equivalent of the structural chemistry of carbon, as exemplified by the Huckel 4n+2 Rule, benzenoid aromatics and graphite, and tetrahedral carbon and diamond, is brought in the structural chemistry of boron by the [[Jemmis mno rules]] which relates polyhedral and macropolyhedral [[boranes]] to [[allotropes of boron]] and boron-rich solids.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Electronic Requirements for Macropolyhedral Boranes|last=Jemmis|first=E. D. |author2=Balakrishnarajan M. M |author3=Pancharatna P. D.|journal=Chem. Rev.|year=2002|volume=102|issue=1|pages=93–114|doi=10.1021/cr990356x|pmid=11782130}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Analogies between Boron and Carbon|last=Jemmis|first=E. D.|author2=Jayasree E. G.|journal=Acc. Chem. Res.|year=2003|volume=36|issue=11|pages=816–824|doi=10.1021/ar0300266|pmid=14622028}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Electronic structure and bonding of β-rhombohedral boron using cluster fragment approach|last=Prasad|first=D. L. V. K. |author2=Balakrishnarajan M. M |author3=Jemmis E. D.|journal=Phys. Rev. B|year=2005|volume=72|issue=19|article-number=195102|doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.72.195102|bibcode=2005PhRvB..72s5102P}}</ref> He has been awarded [[Padma Shri]] in Science and Engineering category (year 2014) by the Government of India.<ref>{{cite web|title=Padma Shri Award Recipients 2014|url=http://www.pib.nic.in/newsite/erelease.aspx?relid=79881}}</ref>

==Education==
Jemmis, after obtaining his B.Sc. from University College, Thiruvananthapuram and [[St. Thomas College, Thrissur]] and his M.Sc. from [[IIT Kanpur]], joined [[Princeton University]] (1973) under the supervision of Profs [[Paul von Rague Schleyer]] and [[John Pople]] (1998 Nobel laureate). Moving along with his supervisors, Jemmis spent one semester at [[LMU Munich]] and four semesters at the [[University of Erlangen–Nuremberg]]. He was awarded a PhD degree (1978) from Princeton. After a two-year postdoctoral work at [[Cornell University]] with Professor [[Roald Hoffmann]] (1981 Nobel laureate), he joined the School of Chemistry, [[University of Hyderabad]] (1980) rising to the rank of professor (1990) and dean (2002). Jemmis was a visiting fellow at the [[Australian National University]], Canberra (1991) and a visiting professor at the Centre for Computational Quantum Chemistry of the University of Georgia, Athens (2000). Jemmis is an honorary professor at [[JNCASR]] and an adjunct professor at ICTS-TIFR. In 2005, he accepted an invitation from the [[Indian Institute of Science]] (IISc), Bangalore, and joined the Department of Inorganic and Physical Chemistry. In 2008, Jemmis moved again, this time on a five-year deputation, accepting the responsibility to start the [[Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Thiruvananthapuram]] and served there till 2013.

==Research==
Jemmis is engaged in the study of structure and reactivity of molecules, clusters and solids using theoretical methods. A constant attempt is made by his group to find common threads between problems of different areas, viz. between organic and organometallic chemistry; amongst the chemistry of various main group elements; between polymorphs of elements and their compounds; etc. His research group not only gets numbers as an answer to a problem, but also tries to find out why the numbers turn out the way they do, based on overlap of orbitals, perturbation theory and symmetry, and devise transferable models. Significant results have been obtained in understanding the reactions of transition metal [[organometallic]]s, week [[hydrogen bond|H-bond]],<ref>{{cite journal|title=Red-, Blue-, or No-Shift in Hydrogen Bonds: A Unified Explanation|last=Jorly|first=J.|author2=Jemmis E. D.|journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc.|year=2007|volume=129|issue=15|pages=4620–4632|doi=10.1021/ja067545z|pmid=17375920}}</ref> electronic structure of three-dimensional [[aromaticity|aromatic]] compounds,<ref name="Jemmis 1982 7017–7020"/><ref>{{cite journal|title=Aromaticity in three dimensions. 4. Influence of orbital compatibility on the geometry and stability of capped annulene rings with six interstitial electrons|last=Jemmis|first=E. D.|author2=Schleyer P. v. R.|journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc.|year=1982|volume=104|issue=18|pages=4781–4788|doi=10.1021/ja00382a008}}</ref> polyhedral [[boranes]], [[carboranes]], silaboranes, [[Polyhedral skeletal electron pair theory|electron counting rules]] for polycondensation, and structure of [[boron]] allotropes.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Polyhedral Boranes and Elemental Boron: Direct Structural Relations and Diverse Electronic Requirements|last=Jemmis|first=E. D.|author2=Balakrishnarajan M. M.|journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc.|year=2001|volume=123|issue=18|pages=4324–4330|doi=10.1021/ja0026962|pmid=11457199}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=A Unifying Electron-Counting Rule for Macropolyhedral Boranes, Metallaboranes, and Metallocenes|last=Jemmis|first=E. D.|journal=Angew. Chem. Int. Ed.|year=2008|volume=47|issue=30|pages=5561–5564|doi=10.1002/anie.200801295|pmid=18567034}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Stuffed fullerenelike boron carbide nanoclusters|last=Prasad|first=D. L. V. The [[Jemmis mno rules]] for polyhedral boranes have found a place in textbooks <ref>{{cite book|author1=Gary L. Miessler |author2=Donald A. Tarr |title=Inorganic Chemistry|year=2011|publisher=Prentice Hall|isbn=978-0-13-612866-3}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author1=Wai-Kee Li |author2=Gong-Du Zhou |author3=Thomas Mak |title=Advanced Structural Inorganic Chemistry (International Union of Crystallography Texts on Crystallography)|year=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-921695-6}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Thomas Fehlner, Jean-François Halet, Jean-Yves|title=Molecular clusters: a bridge to solid-state chemistry|year=2007|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge|isbn=978-0-521-85236-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author1=Matthias Driess|author2=Heinrich Nöth|title=Molecular clusters of the main group elements|year=2004|publisher=Wiley-VCH|location=Weinheim|isbn=978-3-527-30654-1|edition=1. Just as the basic tenets of the structural chemistry of carbon has stood the test of time, and led to major developments in carbon, the edifice of the structural chemistry expounded by Jemmis has already begun to do so for boron. Several of his predictions have been proved experimentally.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Phase Stabilization through Electronic Tuning: Electron-Poorer Alkali-Metal−Indium Compounds with Unprecedented In/Li Clusters|last=Bin |first=Li|author2=John D. Corbett|journal=J. Am. Chem. Soc.|year=2005|volume=127|issue=3 |pages=926–932|doi=10.1021/ja0402046|pmid=15656631}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=closo-[B21H18]−: A Face-Fused Diicosahedral Borate Ion|last=Bernhardt|first=E.|author2=Brauer D. Ed.|year=2007|volume=46|issue=16|pages=2927–2930|doi=10.1002/anie.200604077|pmid=17366499}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Binary Boron-Rich Borides of Magnesium: Single-Crystal Investigations and Properties of MgB7 and the New Boride Mg5B44|last=Pediaditakis|first=A. |author2=Schroeder M. |author3=Sagawe V |author4=Ludwig T. |author5=Hillebrecht H.|journal=Inorg. Chem.|year=2010|volume=49|issue=23|pages=10882–10893|doi=10.1021/ic1012389|pmid=21043472}}</ref> He has mentored 20 PhD students and several postdoctoral and students and research associates, and published about 200 research articles.
